facts.fact_text: Immediately after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election, Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square (also known as Opera Square) in central Yerevan to protest against alleged irregularities in the election process.
From 20 February 2008 onwards, nationwide daily protest rallies were held by Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters, with their main meeting place being Freedom Square and the surrounding park in Yerevan.
The rallies at Freedom Square, held during the daytime and late into the night, attracted at times tens of thousands of people.
Several hundred demonstrators stayed at Freedom Square around the clock, having set up a camp.
The applicant was an active participant in the rallies at Freedom Square and was often on the podium.
The applicant made a speech on the first day of the rallies at Freedom Square.
On the night of 29 February 2008 the applicant camped at Freedom Square.
The applicant alleged that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m. the police arrived at Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that the several hundred demonstrators camping at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 were mostly still asleep when the police arrived, although some were awake, having been informed in advance about the arrival of a large number of police officers.
The applicant alleged that in total about 800 heavily armed police officers appeared at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.
The applicant alleged that the police cordon started approaching the tents at Freedom Square and panic broke out among the demonstrators who started waking the others up.
The applicant alleged that some of the demonstrators managed to switch on the microphones and the lights on Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was also at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 and addressed the demonstrators, saying: "We see that police forces have arrived at the square. Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".
The applicant alleged that after Mr Ter-Petrosyan's address there was silence for about a minute, by which time the police forces had already encircled Freedom Square with a triple cordon.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.
The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was immediately arrested and taken away from Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.
The applicant alleged that within a few minutes no demonstrator remained at Freedom Square, since everybody, including the applicant, had tried to save themselves by fleeing.
The applicant alleged that he and other activists were then pursued by the police through the streets and arrested.

The state of emergency declared by President Kocharyan prohibited, inter alia, the holding of any further rallies and other mass public events for a period of twenty days.

Section 10 §§ 1, 2 and 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that, except for cases when a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event, mass public events may be held only after notifying the competent authority in writing.

Section 10 § 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the organisers shall submit a written notification of the intention to hold a mass public event to the head of the local authority where the event is to be held or to the Mayor of Yerevan, if the public event is to be held in Yerevan, not later than five working days and not earlier than twenty days before the planned date of the event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to decide to terminate a public event and to order the organisers to terminate the event, by allowing them a reasonable time-limit to do so, if, inter alia, the mass public event is being held without notification, except for the cases in which a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to terminate forcibly a public event only if (a) the order to terminate an event is not immediately announced to the participants by the organiser; or (b) the order to terminate the public event has not been complied with within the fixed time-limit and its continuation poses a real threat to the life and health of others, State and public security, public order or public or private property.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police, before forcibly terminating an event, are obliged to inform the participants at least twice over a loudspeaker about the order to terminate the public event and to fix a reasonable time-limit for its termination, and that if the public event is not terminated within such a time-limit, the police are entitled to terminate the event forcibly, using lawful means.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.
The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that a number of participants in the mass events at Freedom Square illegally possessed and carried illegally obtained arms and ammunition.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

After Freedom Square was cleared of demonstrators on 1 March 2008, some of them relocated to the area near the French Embassy, the Yerevan Mayor's Office and the Yerevan Press Building, situated at Grigor Lusavorich and Arshakunyats Streets about 1.7-2 km from Freedom Square.

The demonstrators who relocated near the French Embassy, the Yerevan Mayor's Office and the Yerevan Press Building were later joined by thousands of others who apparently poured into the streets of Yerevan in response to the events of the early morning of 1 March 2008 to voice their discontent.
The rallies on 1 March 2008 continued throughout the city of Yerevan until late at night, involving clashes between protesters and law enforcement officers.

On 2 March 2008 another criminal case was instituted, no. 62202608, under Article 225 § 3 and Article 235 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code, in connection with the events following the clearing of Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202608 stated that Mr Ter-Petrosyan, the candidate running for president at the 19 February 2008 presidential election, and his followers and supporters, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others, not willing to concede defeat at the election, with the aim of casting doubt on the election and discrediting the election and the authorities, from 1 March 2008 in the area of the Yerevan Mayor's Office and central streets organised mass disorder involving murders, violence, pogroms, arson, destruction of property and armed resistance to public officials, with the use of firearms, explosives and other adapted objects.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that from 20 February 2008 onwards the applicant, together with Mr Ter-Petrosyan and others, organised and conducted unlawful public events, mass demonstrations, 24-hour long rallies, assemblies, pickets and sit-ins disrupting the normal life, traffic, functioning of public and private institutions and peace and quiet of the population in Yerevan and involving calls for a violent overthrow of the government and public insults addressed at public officials connected with the performance of their official duties.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police officers demanded the participants in the demonstration at Freedom Square to give a possibility to verify the veracity of the information that they possessed arms and ammunition, and once again warned them to end the unlawful event, the applicant and other demonstrators, disobeying the police officers' lawful orders, committed life- and health-threatening assault on them.

The supplemented charge stated that the applicant, having regularly participated in the unauthorised demonstrations held following the presidential election, had been present at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. when some of the demonstrators, using makeshift clubs, rods and other dangerous objects, had assaulted the police officers after the latter had demanded to be allowed to verify the information concerning the possession of arms and ammunition by the demonstrators.

The supplemented charge stated that the applicant had refused to comply with the lawful orders of the police officers, assaulted police officer A.Arsh., twice hitting him on the head with a stick and causing light damage to his health, after which he had disappeared in the crowd.

The Government claimed that the reason for the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square was information obtained on 29 February 2008 by the Armenian Police and National Security Service, according to which a large number of weapons, including metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives, were to be distributed to the protesters to incite provocative actions and mass disorder in Yerevan on 1 March 2008.
The Government claimed that the police operation of 1 March 2008 aimed to verify the intelligence information about weapons being distributed to protesters.

The Government claimed that the demonstrators attacked the police officers on 1 March 2008, hitting them and throwing stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails at them, as a result of which numerous police officers were injured.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that in the period preceding 1 March 2008 intelligence information was received by the Armenian Police and the National Security Service that the demonstrators gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square had in their possession firearms, ammunition, clubs, rods and other objects for the purpose of causing physical injuries and violence.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. police officers demanded the persons gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square to allow them to verify the above information by inspecting the area, and that this demand was announced out loud several times.

The supplemented charge stated that the applicant, having regularly participated in the unauthorised demonstrations held following the presidential election, had been present at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. when some of the demonstrators, using makeshift clubs, rods and other dangerous objects, had assaulted the police officers after the latter had demanded to be allowed to verify the information concerning the possession of arms and ammunition by the demonstrators.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.

The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was also at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 and addressed the demonstrators, saying: "We see that police forces have arrived at the square. Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".

The Government claimed that the demonstrators attacked the police officers on 1 March 2008, hitting them and throwing stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails at them, as a result of which numerous police officers were injured.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the campaign headquarters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan and the opposition Heritage Party both insisted that the objective of the measures of the morning of 1 March 2008 was, under the disguise of an inspection of the area, to terminate by force the peaceful demonstrations that had been ongoing for ten days, to remove the persons participating in the sit-in and to ban further demonstrations at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report noted contradictions in the statements released by the Prosecutor General's Office, including that the request lodged by the Prosecutor General on 4 March 2008 stated "the objective of the police was to carry out an operation aimed at seizing arms, which deteriorated into a clash", while the press release issued by the Prosecutor General's Office on 1 March stated "the objective of the police was to terminate forcibly the assembly at around 6 a.m. on 1 March".

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that while it is true that every day prior to 1 March the police announced over loudspeakers that the demonstration was unlawful and ordered the demonstrators to end it, no such order was made in the morning of 1 March 2008 and no time-limit was given to the demonstrators to end the demonstration as required by section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the search operation reportedly started early Saturday morning at approximately 6.30 a.m., during which tents were taken down and people were beaten and injured, and that demonstrators started resisting and clashes broke out.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to multiple witnesses, even before Mr Ter-Petrosyan finished his address, police advanced towards the demonstrators in several lines, beating their truncheons against their plastic shields, making no audible demand for anyone to disperse nor giving any indication of the purpose of their presence, and then without any warning, riot police attacked the demonstrators, using rubber truncheons, iron sticks, and electric shock batons.
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that to date, not a single criminal case had been initiated against any police officer, even for excessive use of physical force and of special means.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) deplored the clashes between the police and the protesters and the escalation of violence on 1 March 2008 which resulted in 10 deaths and about 200 people being injured, and stated that the exact circumstances that led to the tragic events of 1 March, as well as the manner in which they were handled by the authorities, including the imposition of a state of emergency in Yerevan from 1 to 20 March 2008 and the alleged excessive use of force by the police, should be the subject of a credible independent investigation.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) urged the Armenian authorities to guarantee freedom of assembly in both law and practice, in compliance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and to stop arbitrary arrests and detentions, as well as the ill-treatment of detainees, in particular during police custody.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that practically all the persons who had been detained by law enforcement officers on 1 March 2008 alleged that they had been physically ill-treated at the time of their apprehension, even though they apparently had not offered resistance, with the ill-treatment consisting mainly of truncheon blows, kicks and punches to the body and head, and being pushed to the ground and dragged into a police vehicle.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that it seemed clear that excessive use of force was used by police and the security forces, as confirmed by the sheer number of injured persons and passing civilians registered in the hospitals as well as found in places of detention, having beating marks, concussion and open scars on their skulls.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that detainees claimed that the police had used excessive force in connection with arrest, and that it seemed that beating took place in a number of cases at the time of arrest and during transportation of the apprehended to the different precincts.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Summary of Findings of 29 September 2008 stated that to date, no law enforcement officials had been charged in connection with the 1 March 2008 events.
